Anuruddha Dharmaratne with lndika Jayaweera for
Counsel appearing for the 6th, th, 2th , 28th & 29th Defendant-
Appellants made submissions on their behalf.
Both counsel submitted that there are other Appellants who have
filed Petitions of Appeal but they are not being represented today. Several
notices had been sent by the Registrar of this Court directing them to be
present in Court to pursue their appeals. Those other Appellants are the
I l i I l i ,,
14th & 23rd Defendants in the District Court. Counsel also submitted that
the grounds of appeal in those appeals also are similar to the grounds that
are being argued today. In the light of the above, Court decides to
consider the merits of this appeal even though the other Appellants are
not present in Court to pursue their appeals.
By this appeal, the Appellants sought to set aside the order of the
learned District Judge made on 28.09.1998. By that order, the application
made in the Petition dated 31.07.1997 had been allowed. Application
made in that petition by three Petitioners, had been made claiming them
as the heirs of the original 4th defendant.
The aforesaid Petition dated 31.07.1997 was made in terms of
Section 48(4) of the Partition Act No. 21 of 1977. Accordingly, learned
District Judge should have granted special leave at the first instance in view
of Section 48(4) ( c ), before he makes a final order on the said application.
Section 48 (4) (c) of the Partition Act reads thus:
(c) If upon inquiry into such application, after prior notice to the parties
to the action deriving any interest under the interlocutory decree
the court shall upon such terms and conditions as the court in its
discretion may impose, which may include an order for payment of
costs as well as an order for security for costs, grant special/eave to
At this stage, both counsel concede that the learned District Judge
had over looked granting special leave referred to in the said section 48(4)
( c ) of the Partition Act. They further submit that no such leave had been
granted by the learned District Judge in this instance. Therefore, it is clear
that the learned District Judge had not followed the procedure referred to
in Section 48{4)( c) of the Partition Act.
However, having considered the reasons in the order dated
28.09.1998, it is now clear that the learned District Judge should have made
an order granting special leave to proceed with the application made by the
three Petitioners without making a final order at that stage. Accordingly,
having considered the circumstances under which the application made
under Section 48(4) ( c ) had been made, this Court varies the order dated
Accordingly, this Court makes an order, granting special leave to
proceed with the petition dated 31.07.1997. In the circumstances, the
learned District Judge is directed to follow the procedure found subsequent
to the Section 48(4)( c) of the Partition Act.
For the aforesaid reasons, the impugned order of the learned District
Judge is varied, to the extent mentioned hereinbefore and accordingly, the
appeal is allowed to that extent.
JUDGE OF THE COURT OF APPEAL
